15	
16	# From Lab to Reality: A Practical Evaluation of Deep Learning Models and LLMs for Vulnerability Detection
17	
18	- Authors: Lu, Chaomeng; Lagaisse, Bert
19	- Year / venue: 2025, arXiv (record in metadata.json). **Published version:** Journal of Systems and Software, Nov 2026, doi 10.1016/j.jss.2026.113185 (Elsevier, not OA). The orchestrator verified this via Crossref on 2026-11-12; it is not in metadata.json. Status: **peer-reviewed**.
20	- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2512.10485 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10485
21	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` = arXiv v4, the accepted manuscript ("accepted for publication in the Journal of Systems and Software", footnote p. 1). Page refs = PDF page index of arXiv v4, not JSS pagination.
22	
23	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
24	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
25	
26	## 1. Research objective
27	- [A] Test whether DL vulnerability detectors and LLMs that score well on curated benchmarks still work under deployment-like conditions. The study looks at three things: separability of code representations, within- vs cross-dataset generalisation, and detection of recent, temporally separated vulnerabilities (p. 1, p. 2).
28	- [A] Contribution claimed: VentiVul, a temporally separated out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmark of 200 CVEs / 263 vulnerable–patched pairs, plus a "Whole-File" + "Function-Pair" evaluation protocol (p. 2). "Out-of-distribution" means test data drawn from a different source or period than the training data.
29	
30	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
31	- [A] RQ1: do graph-based and CodeBERT representations separate vulnerable from non-vulnerable code before task-specific training? (p. 6)
32	- [A] RQ2: how do benchmark characteristics affect within-dataset and cross-dataset performance of DL detectors? (p. 7)
33	- [A] RQ3: how well do trained DL models and off-the-shelf LLMs detect recent vulnerabilities on a temporally separated benchmark? (p. 7)
34	- No formal hypotheses.
35	
36	## 3. Methodology
37	- Research design: [V] Controlled empirical evaluation in three stages: representation diagnostics (t-SNE + centroid distance), 4×4 train/test matrix of DL models across datasets, inference-only evaluation on VentiVul (pp. 6–8).
38	- Approach / models: [V] DL: Devign (gated GNN on code property graphs), ReVeal (Joern graphs + token embeddings, SMOTE), LineVul (fine-tuned CodeBERT), VulBERTa (RoBERTa pretrained on C/C++) (p. 5). LLMs, open-weight, no fine-tuning: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite-Instruct (16B MoE, 2.4B active), Qwen3-30B-A3B (thinking mode disabled), Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct-2501, all released before May 2025 (p. 5, p. 8).
39	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] DL vs LLM only on VentiVul. Only ReVeal and LineVul (each trained on the four datasets) were taken to VentiVul; Devign and VulBERTa were not (p. 7). LLM prompting: zero-shot, few-shot (demonstrations drawn from complete vulnerable–patched pairs, the same number from each project; k = 4 is given only "for example", and the k actually used is not stated), chain-of-thought (p. 8, Table 4 p. 9). [I] No SAST tool, no proprietary/frontier LLM, no fine-tuned LLM and no trivial baseline (e.g. all-positive or random) is included.
40	
41	## 4. Dataset and sample
42	- Data source(s): [V] Juliet 253,002 functions, 37% vulnerable, synthetic; Devign 27,318, 46%, manual; BigVul 188,636, 6%, patches; ICVul 15,396, 41%, patches (p. 3, Table 1). All C/C++.
43	- VentiVul: [V] CVEs for Linux and Chromium disclosed from May 1, 2025, taken from NVD in disclosure order until 100 per project; manually verified; target size fixed before collection; "records were not selected based on model predictions" (p. 4). 13,326 functions, 200 CVEs, 39 CWEs, 263 pairs; Chromium 7,095 functions / 100 CVEs / 20 CWEs / 147 pairs; Linux 6,231 / 100 / 27 / 116 (p. 4, Table 2). Pre-fix function = vulnerable, post-fix = non-vulnerable, plus other functions from the same files labelled non-vulnerable to keep realistic imbalance (p. 4).
44	- Sample size (N) and unit: functions (Whole-File), CVEs (CDR) and vulnerable–patched pairs (PACC) (p. 7). [I] Each of the 263 pairs has exactly one vulnerable function (p. 4), so prevalence p = 263/13,326 = 1.97%. The Table 7 numbers confirm this: back-calculating prevalence from accuracy, precision and recall gives 1.97% for every LineVul row, which matches 263/13,326. The ReVeal rows give 1.79%, because ReVeal is scored only on the functions its preprocessing can handle (p. 7). An all-positive classifier would therefore score F1 = 2p/(1+p) ≈ 3.87% on the full set and ≈ 3.5% on ReVeal's subset (our calculation from p. 4 and Table 7 p. 13).
45	- Sampling / selection method: [V] Inclusion: valid references, explicit fix in non-test C/C++ files, CWE available; excluded: missing references, non-C/C++ or test-only fixes, fixes with "excessive unrelated files or functions" (p. 4). Train/test split ratios for the four benchmarks: not reported.
46	- Data availability: [V] "All of our datasets, code, and results are available" on GitHub (p. 2).
47	
48	## 5. Experimental setup
49	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] DL models use the original authors' code and "recommended settings" (p. 8); H100 GPUs (p. 8). Leakage controls: strict train–test splits with duplicate functions filtered, a fixed test set per target benchmark (p. 7). LLMs run locally via vLLM on B200 GPUs, temperature 0, top-p 1, seed 42, max 384 output tokens, JSON-only binary label; unparseable outputs kept as failures (p. 8). Each model, DL or LLM, receives one function at a time (p. 7, p. 8). Few-shot demonstrations are removed from the test set by pair identifier and code hash (p. 8). ReVeal metrics are computed only over functions its preprocessing can handle (p. 7). Two policies for LLMs: valid-only and conservative (failures counted wrong) (p. 8).
50	- Code availability: [V] public GitHub repository (p. 2).
51	
52	## 6. Evaluation metrics
53	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1 for Whole-File (p. 9). CVE Detection Rate (CDR): share of CVEs with at least one vulnerable function flagged, i.e. CVE-level coverage (p. 9). Patch Pair Accuracy (PACC): share of pairs where the vulnerable version is flagged and the patched version is not, i.e. sensitivity to the fix (p. 9). Centroid distance in min-max normalised t-SNE space, described as descriptive only (pp. 8–9).
54	- Statistical testing: not reported. There are no significance tests or confidence intervals. LLMs use one deterministic run (temperature 0, seed 42, p. 8). For DL training, the number of runs and the random seeds are not reported (p. 8 refers only to the original authors' "recommended settings").
55	
56	## 7. Key findings
57	1. In-distribution DL (within-dataset) — [V] LineVul F1 94.52 and VulBERTa 94.14 on Juliet; LineVul F1 91.00 on BigVul (p. 11; Table 6 p. 12). On BigVul, ReVeal, Devign and VulBERTa reach accuracy 87.45, 94.09, 94.39 but F1 only 23.58, 16.90, 0.19 (p. 11). [A] Because BigVul has a much smaller vulnerable share (6%), "predictions biased toward the non-vulnerable majority class can produce high accuracy while detecting few vulnerable functions" (p. 11).
58	2. Cross-dataset DL — [V] LineVul (Juliet) F1 94.52 in-dataset falls to 53.95 (Devign), 10.73 (BigVul), 51.22 (ICVul) (p. 11). LineVul (BigVul) falls from 91.00 to 0 (Juliet), 1.90 (Devign), 13.05 (ICVul) (p. 12). ReVeal (BigVul) is below 1.00 F1 on all three external sets (p. 11). [A] "No evaluated model consistently preserves its within-dataset performance" (p. 11).
59	3. Temporally separated DL (VentiVul, Whole-File) — [V] F1 3.47–8.65 across the 8 ReVeal/LineVul configurations; best ReVeal (BigVul) F1 8.65 with precision 5.25%, recall 24.43% (p. 13, Table 7). Devign-trained models: recall 99.24–100% but precision about 2% (p. 13, Table 7). LineVul (BigVul) F1 6.87 on VentiVul vs 91.00 in-distribution (Table 7 p. 13; Table 6 p. 12).
60	4. Temporally separated LLMs (VentiVul) — [V] Conservative F1 0.79–5.36 across 4 models × 3 prompts; all conservative F1 < 5.5% and all PACC < 6% (p. 13; Table 8 p. 14). Best: Mistral-Small-24B few-shot F1 5.36%, CDR 46%, PACC 5.75% (p. 13). Highest valid-only F1: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B CoT 8.21% (conservative 3.04%) (p. 14, Table 8). Zero-shot conservative F1: Qwen2.5-Coder 3.72, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite 4.29, Qwen3 3.09, Mistral 4.07 (p. 14, Table 8). LLM precision and recall are not reported, and the LLMs have no in-distribution numbers.
61	5. DL vs LLM on VentiVul (mostly but not exactly the same samples) [V/I] — [V] best DL Whole-File F1 8.65 (ReVeal-BigVul) vs best LLM conservative F1 5.36 (Mistral few-shot) (p. 13; p. 14). Zero-shot LLM CDR (34%, 20%, 9%, 5%) is lower than most DL configurations (p. 13). Best PACC: DL 5.34% vs LLM 5.75% (p. 13). [V] The evaluated samples differ: ReVeal is scored only on functions it can process (p. 7), the few-shot test set excludes pairs used as demonstrations, and valid-only metrics use only parseable outputs (p. 8). [I] F1 against chance (all-positive F1 ≈ 3.87% at p = 1.97%; ≈ 3.5% on ReVeal's subset; §4): the best DL F1 of 8.65 is about 2.5× its chance level, while the best LLM F1 of 5.36 is about 1.4× chance. LineVul (Devign), with recall 100%, precision 2% and F1 3.93, is in effect the all-positive predictor (p. 13, Table 7). [I] PACC against chance: a random labeller that flags a fraction q of functions independently of their content would get PACC = q(1−q), up to 25% at q = 0.5. All observed PACC values (≤ 5.75%, DL and LLM) are far below that, which means the models usually give the vulnerable and the patched version the same label (our reasoning from the PACC definition, p. 9). This matches ding2025vulnerability, where random pair-wise correctness is 22.70% and models fall far below it [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9].
62	6. CDR vs PACC gap — [V] ReVeal (Devign), ReVeal (ICVul), LineVul (Devign) reach CDR 99.10%, 94.59%, 100% but PACC 0.76%, 0%, 0% (p. 13). [A] Detecting a vulnerable function "does not imply" telling it apart from its patch (p. 13).
63	7. Prompting — [V] Few-shot improves Mistral on all three metrics but degrades the other models; CoT raises Qwen2.5-Coder valid-only F1 but lowers its PACC (p. 13). [A] Prompting effects are "model- and metric-dependent" (p. 13).
64	8. Project/CWE variation — [V] All LLMs have higher CDR on Linux than Chromium. DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite zero-shot CDR is 26% on Chromium and 42% on Linux (p. 13). LineVul (BigVul) has CDR 76% on Chromium and 0 on Linux (p. 13). The LLM project-specific results are zero-shot, valid-only (p. 13). Best project-specific PACC is < 8% (LineVul-ICVul 7.48% on Chromium) (p. 14). Per-CWE PACC peaks at 18.18% (LineVul-ICVul, CWE-472) on small cells (p. 14).
65	9. Representations — [V] GNN centroid distances: Juliet 0.0242, ICVul 0.0057, BigVul 0.1612; CodeBERT: BigVul 0.166, Devign 0.0068 (pp. 9–10). [A] Neither representation consistently separates vulnerable from non-vulnerable code (p. 10).
66	
67	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
68	- [A] Only four DL models, two DL families on VentiVul, four open-weight LLMs; no proprietary LLMs; conclusions apply to the evaluated models (p. 17).
69	- [A] LLM pretraining corpora and cutoffs are unknown, so temporal separation "cannot fully exclude training-data contamination" (p. 17).
70	- [A] t-SNE is parameter-sensitive, and centroid distance cannot capture nonlinear structure. RQ1 does not establish a causal link to RQ2/RQ3 performance (p. 17, p. 15).
71	- [A] Dataset characteristics vary simultaneously, so individual causes cannot be isolated. Preprocessing drops some functions, which affects comparability (p. 17).
72	- [A] VentiVul is C/C++ only (Linux, Chromium) and may not generalise to other languages or proprietary code. "Unrelated" functions may hide other vulnerabilities (residual label noise), and regex function extraction can miss complex C/C++ syntax, which mainly affects Whole-File (p. 17).
73	- [A] VentiVul "does not contain every vulnerability reported for the selected project versions" (incomplete coverage) (p. 17).
74	- [A] Model coverage was constrained by reproducibility, experimental consistency and computational feasibility; conclusions apply "to the evaluated models and settings rather than to all existing vulnerability detection techniques" (p. 17).
75	- [A] The Function-Pair setting is "less exposed" to label-noise and extraction threats because it uses manually verified vulnerable functions and their patched versions (p. 17).
76	- [A] ICVul and VentiVul come from open-source projects and may not represent proprietary industrial software (p. 17).
77	
78	## 9. Limitations we identified
79	- [I] No trivial baseline. At p = 263/13,326 = 1.97% (p. 4), an all-positive classifier scores F1 = 2p/(1+p) ≈ 3.87%. All eight DL F1 values (3.47–8.65, Table 7 p. 13) are at most 4.8 points above that. Seven of the 12 LLM conservative F1 values (Table 8 p. 14) fall below it: 3.72, 2.95, 3.04, 3.64, 3.09, 0.79 and 1.39. The paper calls these results "limited" or "weak" (p. 13) but never compares them with chance.
80	- [I] The DL and LLM comparison is asymmetric. DL models were trained on historical data; LLMs were used zero/few-shot without fine-tuning, with small open-weight models (MoE models with 2.4–3B active parameters) and Qwen3 thinking disabled (p. 5, p. 8). The study says nothing about frontier or fine-tuned LLMs, and nothing about LLMs in-distribution, because LLMs were not run on the four benchmarks.
81	- [I] LLM precision/recall are not reported (Table 8 gives F1, CDR, PACC only, p. 14), so we cannot tell whether LLMs fail through false positives or false negatives.
82	- [I] No confidence intervals. LLMs get a single deterministic run (temperature 0, seed 42, p. 8); DL run counts and seeds are not reported. With 263 pairs, PACC differences of a few points (e.g. 5.34% vs 5.75%) are within noise.
83	- [I] One function at a time with no context (p. 7). This is fair between families but disadvantages LLMs, which may need inter-procedural context. With 263 pairs across 200 CVEs (p. 4), at most 63 CVEs have more than one affected function (e.g. CVE-2025-37777, two functions in two files, p. 4). The share of CVEs that need cross-function reasoning is not reported.
84	- [I] No static-analysis tool is evaluated, although the introduction positions learning-based detection as a complement to static analysis (p. 1).
85	- [I] Version: we analyse arXiv v4 (4 Nov 2026), the accepted manuscript (footnote p. 1). The published JSS version (doi 10.1016/j.jss.2026.113185, Crossref-verified 2026-11-12) is not open access and was not compared with it, so small differences between the two versions cannot be ruled out. Page refs follow arXiv v4.
86	
87	## 10. Threats to validity
88	- Internal: [I] Deduplication within datasets and fixed test sets are reported (p. 7), but split ratios and cross-dataset overlap checks are not reported (Devign is from FFmpeg/QEMU and BigVul from open-source C/C++ repositories, p. 3, so project overlap is possible but unchecked). ReVeal is scored only on functions it can process (p. 7), which may inflate or deflate its numbers relative to LineVul. Overlap with training and pretraining data was not checked. Temporal separation covers the CVEs and their fixes (disclosed from May 2025, p. 4). The "unrelated" same-file functions that make up most of VentiVul can be much older code. The paper describes BigVul and ICVul only as drawn from open-source C/C++ repositories and GitHub fix commits (p. 3), and does not say whether they contain older Linux/Chromium code. It reports no check of whether VentiVul functions appear in the DL training sets or in LLM pretraining corpora (pp. 3–4).
89	- Conflict of interest: [I] ICVul, one of the four training benchmarks, is the authors' own dataset (Lu, Li, Dehaene, Lagaisse, MSR 2025; p. 3, reference list p. 18). The paper presents it as "high-quality" (p. 3). Its results are not singled out favourably, but the dependence should be noted. Funding: not reported (no funding or acknowledgement statement in the text).
90	- External: [I] C/C++, two very large projects, 200 CVEs, open-weight mid-size LLMs only (p. 4, p. 5).
91	- Construct: [I] Labelling unrelated same-file functions as non-vulnerable (p. 4) is a realistic construct for "scan the whole file", though label noise remains (p. 17). PACC is a strict and useful measure of patch sensitivity. CDR rewards indiscriminate positive prediction, as the paper itself shows (p. 13).
92	- Statistical conclusion: [I] No tests, single runs, small per-CWE cells (p. 14).
93	- Reproducibility: [I] Good overall: data, code and results are public (p. 2), and the decoding settings are fully given (p. 8). Prompt templates are given (Table 4, p. 9), but the system prompt is only paraphrased (p. 8) and the few-shot demonstrations are not listed in the paper. DL hyper-parameters are given only by reference to the original implementations (p. 8), and DL run counts and seeds are not reported.
94	
95	## 11. Future research directions
96	- Stated by authors [A]: representations and training that emphasise security-relevant changes, e.g. vulnerable–patched pair supervision (p. 16); datasets prioritising reliable labels, diverse patterns and explicit vulnerability–fix links over size (p. 16); complementing within-dataset evaluation with cross-dataset and temporally separated testing, and reporting CDR and patch-pair metrics with function-level metrics (p. 16); studying individual dataset factors, broader ecosystems and "more advanced LLM adaptation strategies" (p. 16).
97	- Suggested by us [I]: run SAST tools and frontier/fine-tuned LLMs on VentiVul with file/repository context and a chance baseline. That would give exactly the same-benchmark LLM vs SAST vs DL comparison our RQ5 identifies as missing.
98	
99	## 12. Relevance to our research
100	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (DL vs LLM on largely shared OOD data), RQ2 (temporal separation, cross-dataset shift, class ratio, accuracy vs F1), RQ4 (per-project and per-CWE variation, C/C++), RQ5 (patch-pair sensitivity, chance baselines).
101	- How it informs our work [I]: This is direct, peer-reviewed (JSS 2026) evidence that in-distribution DL scores do not survive temporal shift. It is consistent with ding2025vulnerability, which shows BigVul-trained models collapse on PrimeVul [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]. LineVul's F1 falls from 91–94.5 in-distribution (p. 12) to 4.39–6.87 on VentiVul, and all 8 DL configurations score 3.47–8.65 (p. 13). On F1, the evaluated open-weight LLMs (≤ 32B) do no better than the shifted DL detectors (0.79–5.36), and both families sit within a few points of the all-positive F1 of ≈ 3.87%. On PACC, both families are far below the random q(1−q) level (up to 25%), i.e. they rarely tell a function apart from its patch. It supports the RQ2 claim that evaluation setup drives the reported ranking. It covers no SAST tool or cost, so it adds nothing for RQ3.
102	
103	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
104	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
105	|---|---|---|---|---|
106	| RQ2 | In-distribution DL F1 is high (LineVul 94.52 Juliet, 91.00 BigVul; VulBERTa 94.14 Juliet) but drops cross-dataset (LineVul-BigVul → 0 / 1.90 / 13.05; LineVul-Juliet → 53.95 / 10.73 / 51.22) | 11, 12 | V | moderate: peer-reviewed (JSS 2026); full 4×4 train/test matrix with deduplication and fixed test sets (p. 7); but a single study, 4 models, DL run count not reported; direction consistent with ding2025vulnerability and chakraborty2024revisiting |
107	| RQ2 | High accuracy hides failure at 6% prevalence: BigVul accuracy 87.45/94.09/94.39 with F1 23.58/16.90/0.19 (ReVeal/Devign/VulBERTa) | 11 | V | moderate: table values from a peer-reviewed study; the accuracy–F1 gap follows arithmetically from the 6% class ratio; single study |

146	
147	- Authors: Tashenova, Zhuldyz; Aitmagambetuly, Aisultan; Urynbassarova, Altyn; Zhetkerbay, Askhat; Amanzholova, Shirin; Kerim, Akerke
148	- Year / venue: 2026, Big Data and Cognitive Computing (published)

151	
152	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.

154	
155	## 1. Research objective
156	[A] To test whether high accuracies reported for learning-based detectors on synthetic corpora and random splits (including the authors' own SentinelCMS, ~93% accuracy on 600 synthetic snippets) transfer to real, disclosed WordPress plugin vulnerabilities. The second aim is to quantify how much duplicate leakage, contradictory labels and in-sample stacking inflated the authors' own first release (p. 2). The paper is a self-correcting re-evaluation prompted by an audit of the first release (p. 2; acknowledgment p. 14).
157	
158	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
159	- [A] RQ1 (transfer): does training on real CVE data beat training on synthetic data? (p. 2)
160	- [A] RQ2 (detector families): how do static, classical and neural detectors compare under duplicate-controlled evaluation? (p. 2)
161	- [A] RQ3 (negatives and granularity): how do the negative-sampling variant and label granularity affect results? (p. 2)
162	- [A] RQ4 (evaluation validity): how much do duplicate leakage and in-sample stacking inflate reported performance? (p. 2)
163	- No formal hypotheses are stated.
164	
165	## 3. Methodology
166	- Research design: [V] Benchmark construction plus a comparative evaluation of ten detector configurations under plugin-grouped five-fold cross-validation on complete held-out folds (p. 1, p. 5–6).
167	- Approach / model / intervention:
168	  - [V] **Static analysis (SAST arm):** a "two-pass intra-procedural analyzer" that propagates taint from user-controlled sources to security-sensitive sinks without sanitisation (p. 5). It is **not named and no version is given** (p. 5). The authors call it "intra-procedural and lexical" (p. 13).
169	  - [I] From the description alone it does not match an established PHP SAST tool (e.g. Pixy, RIPS, Psalm/Phan taint mode, Semgrep), and it is most likely the taint component of the authors' own SentinelCMS (p. 2). The paper says neither; this rests on the missing name/version (p. 5) and the SentinelCMS description (p. 2).
170	  - [V] **Classical ML:** Random Forest and linear SVM on character 2–4-gram TF-IDF (char_wb, max_features 5000) (p. 5–6).
171	  - [V] **Neural:** Bi-LSTM with attention, a unidirectional LSTM ablation, and a "combined" model that concatenates the taint verdict to the Bi-LSTM representation (p. 5).
172	  - [V] **Stacking:** logistic-regression meta-learner, in an in-sample form (the original buggy implementation, kept only to measure bias) and a nested out-of-fold form (the citable one). The LSTM tower is omitted from both (p. 5–6).
173	  - [V] **No LLMs and no pre-trained transformers were run.** CodeBERT was not run "because the transformers library is not installed in the evaluation environment and the host has no GPU" (p. 13). LLMs appear only in related work (p. 3).
174	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Three deliberately trivial baselines (p. 5):
175	  - majority class (always predicts the most frequent training class);
176	  - a source/sink presence rule (the same rule used for label cleaning);
177	  - a one-feature logistic regression on function token count.
178	  - [V] RQ1 also compares a Bi-LSTM trained on the 600-snippet synthetic corpus with real-to-real CV (p. 7).
179	
180	## 4. Dataset and sample
181	- Data source(s): [V] NVD CVE API v2 and CVEProject/cvelistV5. 6666 unique indexed CVE records; 1757 CVEs in 1281 plugins could be resolved to downloadable pre-fix/post-fix source pairs (p. 3). About 54% of indexed CVEs were unrecoverable because old releases/SVN tags were pruned (p. 3).
182	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] PHP functions. 30,860 snippets per variant before de-duplication; 15,294 (Variant A) and 24,917 (Variant B) after leakage control (p. 5, Table 2).
183	  - **Class balance / prevalence:**
184	    - [V] Variant A: Safe/XSS/SQLi/RCE = 3895/8446/2104/849 (p. 5, Table 2), so vulnerable is the majority class; the majority baseline accuracy is 0.745 (p. 9).
185	    - [V] Variant B: 13,396/8531/2142/848 (p. 5, Table 2); majority baseline accuracy 0.538 (p. 8, Table 6).
186	    - [I] Vulnerable prevalence is therefore 74.5% (A) and 46.2% (B) (our calculation from Table 2 counts). Both are far above realistic prevalence because negatives come only from vulnerable plugins: the patched twins of vulnerable functions in Variant A, untouched functions of the same plugin in Variant B (p. 3).
187	  - [V] Test folds are complete and prevalence-preserving; no balancing or subsampling of test folds (p. 6).
188	- Sampling / selection method: [V] Labels come from tree-sitter diffs of vulnerable vs patched versions (p. 3):
189	  - functions touched by the fix are positives and receive the CVE's vulnerability type; untouched functions are negatives;
190	  - Variant A uses the patched twin as the negative; Variant B uses unmodified functions from the same plugin.
191	- Leakage control: [V] An audit of the first release found (p. 4, Table 1):
192	  - duplicate groups crossing folds: 166 groups / 1086 records (A) and 151 / 676 (B);
193	  - contradictory-label groups: 730 / 456 (1852 / 1199 records).
194	  - [V] Three corrections were applied (p. 4):
195	    - all conflicting-label hash groups were removed;
196	    - exact duplicates (SHA-256 of whitespace-normalised code) were merged;
197	    - near-duplicates were grouped into clone families (MinHash over 5-token shingles, Jaccard ≥ 0.9; AST node-type sequences, Jaccard ≥ 0.9) and each family was collapsed to one record.
198	  - [V] Grouping by connected components was rejected because one giant component covered 59.4% (A) / 72.1% (B) of the corpus (p. 4).
199	  - [V] Final folds share 0 hashes, 0 clone families and 0 plugins (p. 5, Table 2).
200	  - [V] All three corrections together reduced the published 30,860 records by 50.4% (A) and 19.3% (B). Clone-family collapse alone removed 11,123 (A) and 3714 (B) records; conflict removal plus exact deduplication left 26,417 / 28,631 before that step (p. 5, Table 2).
201	  - [V] There is no temporal split; all CVEs predate the experiments and no date cut-off is applied (pp. 3–6). [I] Temporal leakage is not addressed; it is less relevant here because no pre-trained model is used.
202	- Label quality: [V] A stratified 400-function expert review (single annotator, blind to the automated verdict) found (p. 11, Table 10):
203	  - HIGH tier precision 73.0% (27/37);
204	  - MEDIUM tier 44.7% (97/217);
205	  - LOW (discarded) tier 0.7% (1/146);
206	  - cleaned subset (HIGH+MEDIUM) 48.8% (124/254).
207	- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Labels, metadata, hashes, folds and a loader script are on GitHub (Aisultan05/wordpress-cve-benchmark) and Zenodo; the audited rebuild is release v2.1.0. Plugin source is not redistributed but reconstructed from WordPress.org (p. 14). [V] A 125-vulnerability / 247-safe expert-verified subset is released (p. 11).

209	## 5. Experimental setup
210	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
211	  - [V] Splits and losses: StratifiedGroupKFold (scikit-learn 1.8.0), 5 folds, seed 42, grouped by plugin slug; class-weighted cross-entropy (p. 6, Table 3).
212	  - [V] LSTM settings (p. 6, Table 3):
213	    - sequence length 128, 40 epochs, embedding 64, hidden 128, 2 layers, dropout 0.3, batch 16, Adam lr 1e-3;
214	    - at most 4000 training records per fold; CPU only.
215	  - [V] RF: 300 trees, balanced class weights. LinearSVC: C 1.0, balanced (p. 6).
216	  - [V] Software: Python 3.14, PyTorch 2.11 (CPU), NumPy 2.4, tree-sitter-php (p. 7).
217	  - [V] The 128-token bound was chosen for tractability, not tuned; its effect is unmeasured (p. 6).
218	  - [V] Granularities: binary, three-class (Safe/SQLi/XSS) and four-class (+RCE), crossed with the two variants, giving six settings (p. 6).
219	  - [V] Result files are keyed to SHA-256 fingerprints of the dataset index and fold file (p. 6).
220	- Code availability: [V] Data, folds, per-fold predictions, scores and fingerprinted results are released (p. 1, p. 14). [I] Whether training code is in the same repository is implied ("released training scripts", p. 6) but the repository was not inspected.

222	## 6. Evaluation metrics
223	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
224	  - [V] Macro-F1 is the headline metric (fold mean ± SD, 95% CI with t, 4 df) (p. 6).
225	  - [V] Also reported: accuracy, per-class precision/recall/F1, vulnerable-class recall and FNR, balanced accuracy, MCC and PR-AUC (p. 6).
226	  - [A] Accuracy is not comparable with the earlier release because collapsing changed the majority class; macro-F1, balanced accuracy and MCC should be used instead (p. 5, Table 2 note).
227	  - [V] **Vulnerable-class F1 alone is not reported for most models** (only per-class F1 for the Variant B four-class setting, p. 9, Table 7). [I] Headline numbers are therefore not directly comparable with the vulnerable-class F1 used by most studies in our corpus.
228	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals):
229	  - [V] Paired tests across folds and across plugins, with Cohen's d; the plugin-level test is "the better-powered" (p. 6).
230	  - [V] Only one comparison is reported in the text: RF vs majority on Variant A macro-F1 is "significant across folds but not across plugins (Wilcoxon p = 0.295, Cohen's d = 0.057)" (p. 9). The only quantified result is the plugin-level one (p = 0.295, d = 0.057); the fold-level test is not named and its p-value is not reported (p. 6, p. 9).
231	  - [I] With only five paired fold observations (p. 6), a two-sided exact Wilcoxon signed-rank test cannot reach p < 0.05 (smallest attainable p = 2/32 = 0.0625), so the fold-level "significant" result must come from a different test (e.g. a paired t-test) or a one-sided test. Basis: standard property of the exact Wilcoxon test at n = 5.
232	  - [V] 95% CIs are reported for Variant B binary (p. 8, Table 6).
233	  - [V] No multiple-comparison correction is mentioned (pp. 6–9).

270	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
271	- [A] The protocol is "duplicate-controlled rather than provably leakage-free"; semantic clones that differ lexically and structurally may persist (p. 13).
272	- [A] About 54% of indexed CVEs were unrecoverable, so the corpus may be biased toward plugins that retain historical versions (p. 13).
273	- [A] Rare-class estimates are unreliable (RCE 848 records in Variant B; several models never predict it); four-class results are indicative only (p. 13).
274	- [A] Neural models trained on ≤4000 records/fold for 40 epochs on CPU, so their numbers are a lower bound (p. 13).
275	- [A] No transformer comparison (CodeBERT not run; no GPU); the 256-token sensitivity run is outstanding (p. 13).
276	- [A] The taint analyser is intra-procedural and lexical (p. 13).
277	- [A] Labels are only about half correct on the positive class, which "bounds what any model trained on them can demonstrate" (p. 13).
278	- [A] The expert sample was labelled by a single annotator, so no inter-annotator agreement is reported (p. 11).
279	
280	## 9. Limitations we identified
281	- [I] **The SAST arm is a weak straw-man for our RQ1.** It is an unnamed in-house intra-procedural lexical analyser (p. 5, p. 13). No established PHP SAST tool (e.g. Psalm taint analysis, Semgrep, RIPS/Pixy descendants) was run. (That CodeQL does not support PHP is our outside knowledge, not stated in the paper.) The "misses about 98%" result cannot be generalised to PHP SAST.
282	- [I] **No LLM arm at all** (p. 3, p. 13). For our review the paper informs SAST-vs-DL and evaluation methodology, not LLM-vs-anything.
283	- [I] **Label precision of the main benchmark is not reported.** The 48.8% figure (p. 11) refers to the cleaned HIGH+MEDIUM subset. The main experiments (Tables 5–6) use the full corpus, which also contains LOW-tier functions found 0.7% genuine (p. 11) and the 13,702 "noisy" discarded pairs (p. 11, Table 11). Genuine-positive precision in the evaluated corpus is therefore plausibly well below 48.8%, but is not reported. This makes every absolute score hard to interpret.
284	- [I] **Macro-F1 headline** mixes Safe-class and vulnerable-class F1. Combined with class proportions that differ between variants (74.5% vs 46.2% vulnerable), this makes cross-variant and cross-paper comparisons fragile.
285	- [I] **Function-level granularity, not repository-level.** It does not test inter-procedural or cross-file detection, which is the core of our G5 interest. The inter-procedural recovery experiment found only 39 paths (p. 11).
286	- [I] **Self-correction context.** The paper corrects the authors' own earlier release after reviewers audited the artifacts (p. 2, p. 14). This is commendable transparency, but it also means the earlier SentinelCMS numbers (~93%, p. 2) should not be cited.
287	- [I] **Minor presentation issues:**
288	  - The statements are in the singular ("The author declares", "The author thanks") for a six-author paper (p. 14).
289	  - Only one comparison is tested in the text, with only the plugin-level p-value given, despite paired tests being described for model comparisons (p. 6, p. 9; see §6).
290	- [I] **No negatives from unrelated code at realistic prevalence.** Both variants draw negatives from vulnerable plugins only, so the deployment false-alarm rate is unknown.
291	
292	## 10. Threats to validity
293	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection):
294	  - [V] Strong exact- and near-duplicate control with verified 0/0/0 cross-fold overlap (p. 5).
295	  - [V] In-sample stacking leakage is measured and corrected (p. 10).
296	  - [A] Semantic clones may remain (p. 13).
297	  - [I] Label noise (≤48.8% genuine positives) is the dominant confound. Diff-based labelling marks every function touched by a fix as vulnerable, including non-security edits (p. 4, p. 11).
298	  - [V] The filtered-subset comparison is confounded by easier test cases (p. 10).
299	- External (generalisability of sample/context):
300	  - [V] WordPress plugins only, PHP only, XSS/SQLi/RCE only (p. 5).
301	  - [A] Survivorship bias toward plugins with retained history (p. 13).
302	  - [I] Results may not transfer to other PHP frameworks (Laravel, Drupal) or to repository-level detection.
303	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?):
304	  - [I] Macro-F1 averages a Safe-class F1 that depends heavily on negative sampling (Variant A vs B).
305	  - [I] Labels measure "touched by a security fix" more than "vulnerable".
306	  - [V] The per-class tables expose degenerate predictors that aggregate scores hide (p. 9).
307	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance):
308	  - [V] 5 folds give only five paired observations; a plugin-level test is used as the better-powered alternative (p. 6).
309	  - [V] CIs are reported for Variant B binary only (p. 8).
310	  - [V] No multiple-comparison correction is reported (pp. 6–10).
311	  - [V] A single seed (42) is used throughout (p. 7).
312	  - [I] Many between-model gaps (e.g. 0.562–0.601 on Variant B binary) have overlapping CIs (p. 8, Table 6).
313	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Good — hyper-parameters (p. 6–7), folds, per-fold predictions, fingerprinted results and a loader script are released (p. 14). Plugin code must be re-downloaded from WordPress.org (p. 14). [I] Reproducibility therefore depends on WordPress.org continuing to host old versions, the same pruning that already lost 54% of CVEs (p. 3).
314	- Funding and conflicts of interest: [V] "This research received no external funding"; no conflicts of interest are declared (p. 14). [I] The study re-evaluates the authors' own SentinelCMS (p. 2), so it is a self-evaluation; however, any bias would run against the authors' own earlier claims (~93% accuracy, p. 2), which the paper largely retracts, so it is unlikely to inflate the reported results.
315	
316	## 11. Future research directions
317	- Stated by authors [A]:
318	  - extend expert review to several thousand functions with ≥2 annotators and adjudication, and evaluate on an expert-verified test set (p. 13);
319	  - use curated feeds that name entry points and sinks (p. 13);
320	  - semantic clone detection (p. 13);
321	  - a fully resourced transformer comparison on identical folds and a 256-token sensitivity run (p. 13);
322	  - require future detectors to clear trivial baselines such as function length (p. 13).
323	- Suggested by us [I]:
324	  - Run established PHP SAST tools (Semgrep PHP rules, Psalm taint mode, Progpilot) and 1–2 open LLMs on the released expert-verified 125/247 subset (p. 11). That would give a small but clean PHP LLM-vs-SAST-vs-ML comparison, directly addressing G5 and G2.
325	  - Report vulnerable-class F1 and precision at realistic prevalence alongside macro-F1.
326	
327	## 12. Relevance to our research
328	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2 (primary), RQ1 (SAST vs ML/DL only; no LLM), RQ4 (PHP; per-CWE-class behaviour), RQ5.
329	- How it informs our work [I]:
330	  - **RQ2:** a clean demonstration that duplicate leakage, contradictory labels, in-sample stacking and label noise shape measured performance more than model family. It is also a second study (beside shu2026evaluating) that reports trivial baselines and finds they are competitive, which strengthens G1.
331	  - **G5 (PHP):** gives real-CVE PHP evidence, but at function level and without LLMs or a standard SAST tool. The released corpus and expert-verified subset are a ready data source for a G5 study. G5 stays open only pending a novelty check against a likely competitor: Neef et al. 2026 (arXiv:2606.21397, "Evaluating LLMs for Real-World Web Vulnerability Detection"), which deininger2026open cites as comparing models on "web vulnerability detection in WordPress plugins" [@deininger2026open, p. 3]. It is not in our corpus and was not read; its content is unknown beyond that citation.
332	  - **G2:** the closest PHP analogue to a leakage-controlled same-benchmark comparison, missing the LLM arm.
333	  - **RQ4:** XSS is detected far better than RCE by learned models (p. 9), and SQLi per-class F1 is ≤ 0.146 (p. 9, Table 7). This is a hint that rare classes are effectively undetected by small ML models on PHP.
334	  - **C5 (class balance):** the choice of negatives flips the majority class and the failure direction of the same RF model (p. 9).

383	# ChatGPT for Vulnerability Detection, Classification, and Repair: How Far Are We?
384	
385	- Authors: Fu, Michael; Tantithamthavorn, Chakkrit Kla; Nguyen, Van; Le, Trung
386	- Year / venue: 2023, 2023 30th Asia-Pacific Software Engineering Conference (APSEC) (published)
387	- DOI: 10.1109/apsec60848.2023.00085 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1109/apsec60848.2023.00085
388	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
389	
390	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
391	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
392	
393	## 1. Research objective
394	- [A] To assess how well prompted ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo and gpt-4) performs on four vulnerability tasks (function- and line-level vulnerability prediction, CWE-type classification, CVSS severity estimation, vulnerability repair) compared with smaller language models fine-tuned for these tasks (p. 1).
395	- [A] Motivation: ChatGPT's weights are proprietary, so the authors cannot fine-tune it; the comparison is therefore prompted ChatGPT vs fine-tuned code LMs (p. 1).
396	
397	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
398	- [A] RQ1 accuracy of ChatGPT for function- and line-level vulnerability prediction; RQ2 for vulnerability-type (CWE-ID) classification; RQ3 for severity (CVSS) estimation; RQ4 for automated vulnerability repair (p. 1–2).
399	- No formal hypotheses.
400	
401	## 3. Methodology
402	- Research design: [V] Benchmark comparison on held-out test splits of existing datasets; ChatGPT used via prompting through the paid OpenAI API; baselines replicated with the original authors' parameter settings (p. 3).
403	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] gpt-3.5-turbo and gpt-4 with task prompts (Fig. 1–4). Detection: task description plus return-format instruction; for vulnerable functions a follow-up prompt asks for the top-10 most vulnerability-prone lines (p. 2). Classification: ChatGPT is told the function is vulnerable and given a list of candidate CWE-IDs (p. 2). Repair: prompt includes three repair examples (p. 3). [I] The detection prompt appears to be zero-shot (based on the description on p. 2; the prompt itself is only shown as a figure).
404	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] AIBugHunter (fine-tuned LMs, ~120M parameters), CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT (all fine-tuned); VulExplainer added for CWE classification (p. 3–4). [V] No static-analysis (SAST) tool baseline is included (p. 3).
405	
406	## 4. Dataset and sample
407	- Data source(s): [V] Big-Vul (Fan et al.) for RQ1–RQ3: 188k C/C++ functions from 348 GitHub projects, 3,754 vulnerabilities across 91 types, vulnerable functions labelled with CWE-ID and CVSS score, vulnerable:benign ratio 1:20 (p. 3). [V] Big-Vul + CVEFixes as pre-processed by Chen et al. for repair: 5.5k vulnerable-function/patch pairs (p. 3).
408	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] Function. Big-Vul split 80/10/10 (train/val/test); repair data split 70/10/20 (p. 3). The number of test functions actually submitted to ChatGPT is not reported.
409	- Sampling / selection method: [V] Split "similar to previous studies" (p. 3); no de-duplication or time-based split is reported.
410	- Data availability (public? link?): [A] Dataset, prompts and results published at https://github.com/awsm-research/ChatGPT4Vul (p. 1).
411	
412	## 5. Experimental setup
413	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Baselines replicated with original settings on AMD Ryzen 9 5950X, 64 GB RAM, RTX 3090 (p. 3). [V] Greedy decoding for fine-tuned repair models "to ensure a fair comparison with ChatGPT" (p. 5). ChatGPT temperature, model snapshot/date and number of runs: not reported.
414	- Code availability: [A] repository above (p. 1).
415	
416	## 6. Evaluation metrics
417	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] F1, precision, recall (function level) and top-10 accuracy (share of vulnerable functions with at least one true vulnerable line in the top-10 ranking), following LineVul (p. 3); multiclass accuracy for CWE classification (p. 4); MSE and MAE for CVSS v3.1 estimation (p. 4); %PP (exact match with ground-truth patch), BLEU and METEOR for repair (p. 4–5).
418	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): not reported (single point estimates in bar charts).
419	
420	## 7. Key findings
421	1. Function-level detection, Big-Vul test split, F1: AIBugHunter 94%, CodeBERT 87%, GraphCodeBERT 35%, gpt-4 29%, gpt-3.5-turbo 10% — [V] (p. 4, Fig. 5; text p. 3).
422	2. Precision: AIBugHunter 98%, CodeBERT 92%, GraphCodeBERT 50%, gpt-4 25%, gpt-3.5-turbo 11%. Recall: AIBugHunter 90%, CodeBERT 83%, gpt-4 33%, GraphCodeBERT 27%, gpt-3.5-turbo 9% — [V] (p. 4, Fig. 5).
423	3. Line-level top-10 accuracy: AIBugHunter 99%, CodeBERT 99%, GraphCodeBERT 87%, gpt-4 65%, gpt-3.5-turbo 25% — [V] (p. 4, Fig. 5; text p. 3).
424	4. CWE-ID classification accuracy: fine-tuned baselines 62–65% (AIBugHunter 65%, VulExplainer 65%, CodeBERT 63%, GraphCodeBERT 62%) vs gpt-4 20% and gpt-3.5-turbo 13% — [V] (p. 4, Fig. 6).
425	5. CVSS severity: MSE 1.8–1.86 for fine-tuned baselines vs 5.4 (gpt-3.5-turbo) and 5.85 (gpt-4); MAE 0.83–0.93 vs 1.84 and 1.86 — [V] (p. 4, Fig. 7).
426	6. Repair %PP: AIBugHunter (VulRepair) 30, GraphCodeBERT 9, CodeBERT 7, gpt-3.5-turbo 0, gpt-4 0 — [V] (p. 5, Fig. 8).
427	7. Despite ~14,000× more parameters than CodeBERT, ChatGPT needs domain-specific fine-tuning to generalise to vulnerability tasks — [A] (p. 1, p. 5).
428	
429	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
430	- [A] None. The paper has no limitations or threats-to-validity section; the only constraint mentioned is that ChatGPT's parameters are proprietary and cannot be fine-tuned (p. 1).
431	
432	## 9. Limitations we identified
433	- [I] Short paper (5 PDF pages including references): method detail is thin — number of test samples sent to ChatGPT, temperature, model snapshot dates, repeated runs and the full detection prompt text are not given in the text.
434	- [I] Evaluation uses a random Big-Vul split with no de-duplication or temporal split. Ding et al. report 12.7% exact-copy leakage for Big-Vul [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4]; Big-Vul vulnerable-label accuracy is ~25% per Chen et al., as reported by [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4], and 39% in Risse et al.'s own n=100 audit [@risse2025top, p. 8]; Risse et al. also reach 86% F1 on Big-Vul from word counts alone; both suggest the 94% F1 of the fine-tuned baseline is inflated by dataset artefacts that in-distribution fine-tuning can exploit but prompting cannot. The size of the LLM-vs-fine-tuned gap may therefore partly reflect benchmark artefacts (based on [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4] and [@risse2025top, p. 11]).
435	- [I] Asymmetric comparison: baselines are fine-tuned on Big-Vul training data, ChatGPT is prompted. The result answers "prompting vs in-distribution fine-tuning", not "LLM vs DL" in general.
436	- [I] The first two authors also built the strongest baselines (AIBugHunter, LineVul, VulRepair, VulExplainer — refs [8]–[11], p. 5). Not a funding conflict, but the comparison favours the authors' own tools and should be read with that in mind.
437	- [I] GraphCodeBERT F1 35% vs CodeBERT 87% on the same data is an unusually large gap that the paper does not discuss (p. 4, Fig. 5); the dagger marks on CodeBERT/GraphCodeBERT in Fig. 5–7 are not explained in the text.
438	- [I] %PP (exact match) is a very strict repair metric; 0% for ChatGPT may partly reflect format mismatch with Chen et al.'s patch representation, which the authors tried to mitigate with three in-prompt examples (p. 3).
439	
440	## 10. Threats to validity
441	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Random Big-Vul split without reported de-duplication → possible train/test leakage that only benefits the fine-tuned baselines; prompt design not tuned or ablated; single run.
442	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] C/C++ only, one detection dataset, one 2023 snapshot of each ChatGPT model; results may not transfer to newer LLMs, other prompting strategies or other languages.
443	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] F1 on a 1:20 dataset whose vulnerable labels are largely inaccurate per later audits, so "correct" predictions need not be detected vulnerabilities; %PP measures textual identity, not functional correctness.
444	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No variance, confidence intervals or significance tests; LLM outputs are non-deterministic and only one run is implied.
445	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [A] Data, prompts and results released (p. 1); [I] model versions and temperature are not stated, and hosted OpenAI models change over time.
446	
447	## 11. Future research directions
448	- Stated by authors [A] (p. 5): fine-tuning on domain-specific data is "crucial" for ChatGPT to generalise to vulnerability repair, and "pivotal" for vulnerability tasks in general.
449	- Suggested by us [I]: re-run the prompted-LLM vs fine-tuned comparison on a de-duplicated, temporally split, label-verified benchmark (e.g. PrimeVul), add a SAST baseline, and report variance across repeated LLM runs.
450	
451	## 12. Relevance to our research
452	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ4.
453	- How it informs our work [I]: An early, widely cited head-to-head of prompted ChatGPT vs fine-tuned code LMs showing a large gap in favour of fine-tuned models on Big-Vul. For RQ2 it illustrates how a random-split Big-Vul evaluation can make fine-tuned models look near-perfect. It should be read together with ding2025vulnerability, where the ordering reverses only under a different metric and test set: on 564 PrimeVul pairs scored by pair-wise correctness (P-C), GPT models beat fine-tuned models, although all are at or below random guessing [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9]. On Big-Vul with F1, Ding's own fine-tuned rows (62.88–68.26%) agree with this paper's direction [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]; the apparent contradiction is therefore one of metric (F1 vs P-C) and dataset (random-split Big-Vul 1:20 vs de-duplicated temporal PrimeVul pairs).
454	
455	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
456	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
457	|---|---|---|---|---|
458	| RQ1 | On Big-Vul (random split), prompted gpt-4 F1 29% and gpt-3.5-turbo F1 10% vs fine-tuned AIBugHunter 94% and CodeBERT 87% for function-level detection | 4 | V | moderate |
459	| RQ1 | Line-level top-10 accuracy: gpt-4 65%, gpt-3.5-turbo 25% vs AIBugHunter/CodeBERT 99% | 4 | V | moderate |
460	| RQ4 | CWE-ID classification accuracy: ChatGPT 13–20% vs fine-tuned models 62–65% (C/C++, Big-Vul) | 4 | V | moderate |
461	| RQ1 | ChatGPT produced 0% exact-match repairs vs 7–30% for fine-tuned models | 5 | V | weak |
462	| RQ2 | Evaluation used an 80/10/10 Big-Vul split (1:20 ratio) with no de-duplication or temporal split reported | 3 | V | moderate |
463	| RQ5 | Authors argue prompted LLMs lack security domain knowledge and need fine-tuning for vulnerability tasks | 5 | A | weak |
464	
465	## 14. Key quotes
466	> "the fine-tuned AIBugHunter achieves an F1-measure of 94% along with a top-10 accuracy of 99% with only 120 million parameters" (p. 3)
467	
468	> "ChatGPT failed to generate correct repair patches for all of the vulnerable functions in our testing data." (p. 5)
469	
470	## Analyst notes
471	- Reading coverage: whole paper read (5 PDF pages: abstract, introduction, related work, prompt design, experiments, conclusion, references). Bar-chart values in Fig. 5–8 were read from the rendered PDF pages 4–5 because text extraction garbles the axis labels.
472	- Source version: arXiv 2310.09810v1 (15 Oct 2023); the published version is APSEC 2023 (DOI above). Page refs are to the arXiv PDF; small differences from the APSEC version are possible.
473	- Short paper (5 pages, self-described "pilot study", p. 2): weight accordingly in synthesis.
474	- Uncertainties: ChatGPT test-set size, full detection prompt (figure only), model snapshot dates and temperature are not reported. In Fig. 5 gpt-4 recall (33%) is above GraphCodeBERT (27%) although its F1 is lower — values read from the rendered figure.

## Vulnerability Detection with Code Language Models: How Far are We?

> **Takeaway:** Popular test sets for AI vulnerability detectors contain many wrong labels and copied test examples, so AI models that look strong on them (F1 up to 68%) mostly fail on a cleaned, time-split benchmark. Even GPT-4 scores below random guessing at telling vulnerable code apart from its fixed version [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7; @ding2025vulnerability, p. 9].

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Authors | Yangruibo Ding, Yanjun Fu, Omniyyah Ibrahim, Chawin Sitawarin, Xinyun Chen, Basel Alomair, David Wagner, Baishakhi Ray, Yizheng Chen |
| Year | 2025 |
| Venue | 2025 IEEE/ACM 47th International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE) |
| Status | Peer-reviewed (ICSE 2025). Our copy is the arXiv version (2403.18624v2), so page numbers follow the arXiv PDF |
| Identifier | DOI 10.1109/icse55347.2025.00038; arXiv 2403.18624 |
| Paper type | Dataset audit, new benchmark (PrimeVul) and experiments with 7 code language models |
| Relevance to us | High (RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ5) |

### In plain words
A vulnerability is a flaw in code that an attacker can exploit. Researchers train AI models to spot such flaws. They train and test them on benchmarks: large collections of functions labelled "vulnerable" or "safe". A function is a small, named block of code. This paper asks whether those benchmarks can be trusted. The answer is mostly no. Many labels are wrong, and many test functions also appear in the training data. The authors build a cleaner benchmark called PrimeVul and test the models again. Scores collapse. They also test GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. These are large language models (LLMs): very big AI models trained on huge amounts of text and code.

### How they did it
- Label audit: three people checked 50 random "vulnerable" functions per benchmark and took a majority vote [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 3].
- Leakage check: data leakage means a test example also sits in the training data, so a model can simply remember it. The authors compared every test function with the training set after removing spaces and line breaks [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4].
- PrimeVul: they merged four existing datasets. They kept only functions with stronger evidence that they really were the vulnerable code. They removed exact copies. They split the data by time: the oldest 80% of code changes for training, the next 10% for tuning, the newest 10% for testing [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 5; @ding2025vulnerability, p. 6].
- Models: five open code models were fine-tuned, which means given extra training on this task. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 were prompted with two examples ("two-shot") or asked to reason step by step ("chain-of-thought"). GPT-3.5 was also fine-tuned [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7].
- New scores: VD-S is the share of real vulnerabilities a model misses when its false-alarm rate is held at 0.5% or less. Pair-wise scores test a vulnerable function together with its fixed (patched) version. "P-C" means both were labelled correctly [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 6].
- No static analysis tool was tested [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]. Static analysis (SAST) tools scan code with fixed rules without running it.

### Data and setup
- PrimeVul holds 6,968 vulnerable and 228,800 safe C/C++ functions from 755 projects, covering 140 CWEs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 6]. A CWE is a standard category of weakness, such as a buffer overflow.
- The test set has 695 vulnerable and 25,216 safe functions, about 1 vulnerable for every 32 safe [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 6; @ding2025vulnerability, p. 8].
- Because of cost, the GPT models were run only on 564 test pairs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9].
- The number of repeated runs and random seeds is not reported. Data, code and prompts are released [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 3].

### Key findings
- [V] In the authors' own audit, only 24% (CodeXGLUE/Devign) and 36% (VulnPatchPairs) of "vulnerable" labels were correct, against 86–92% for PrimeVul [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4]. The BigVul figure of 25% in the same table comes from an earlier study, not from this audit [A].
- [V] Exact copies from training into test reach 12.7% in BigVul and 18.9% in CVEFixes; PrimeVul has 0.0% [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4].
- [V] F1 is a 0–100% score that balances precision (how many alarms are real) and recall (how many real flaws are found). Fine-tuned models score F1 62.88–68.26% on BigVul, 18.05–21.43% when trained and tested on PrimeVul, and 1.91–5.82% when trained on BigVul and tested on PrimeVul [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7].
- [I] The often-quoted drop from 68.26% to 3.09% mixes two effects: a cleaner test set and a switch to a different dataset. The fair within-PrimeVul figure is 18.05% [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7].
- [V] At a false-alarm rate of 0.5% or less, PrimeVul-trained models miss 88.78–91.51% of vulnerabilities [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7].
- [V] Extra training tricks (class weights, contrastive learning) raise one model's F1 from 21.43% to at most 26.28%, but it still misses at least 88% of vulnerabilities [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 8; @ding2025vulnerability, p. 9].
- [V] Pair-wise correctness on 564 pairs: GPT-4 chain-of-thought 12.94%, GPT-3.5 chain-of-thought 6.21%, fine-tuned GPT-3.5 1.24%, fine-tuned open models 1.06–3.01%. Random guessing scores 22.70% [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7; @ding2025vulnerability, p. 9].
- [V] The two families fail in opposite ways. GPT-4 two-shot calls both versions vulnerable in 71.63% of pairs, while fine-tuned open models call both safe in 84.22–88.30% [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7; @ding2025vulnerability, p. 9].

### Limitations and weaknesses
- [A] The authors note that PrimeVul labels are still not 100% correct, that VD-S depends on the chosen 0.5% threshold, and that OpenAI models ran with default settings. They also say a function without its surrounding code may be "an impossible question" even for humans [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 10].
- [I] GPT models and fine-tuned models are never scored on the same metric. GPT models were run on pairs only, so there is no F1 or VD-S for them [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9].
- [I] Fine-tuning of GPT-3.5 was weak (one training pass on a 1:3 subsample), so its poor result says little about well-tuned LLMs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9].
- [I] Only exact copies were removed; near-copies with renamed variables may remain. Audits used 50 functions each, which leaves wide uncertainty (about plus or minus 14 points).
- [I] The text gives CodeBERT accuracy as 96.86% on BigVul, but the table shows 95.57% [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7; @ding2025vulnerability, p. 8]. There are no repeated runs or confidence intervals.

### Gaps and future work this paper leaves open
- Gap G1 (no shared evaluation protocol): the paper proposes VD-S because accuracy and F1 mislead [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 2], and its random-guess row shows why every result needs a chance reference.
- Gap G2 (no same-benchmark LLM vs SAST vs deep-learning comparison): PrimeVul has no SAST arm, and the GPT models were tested on pairs only.
- [A] The authors call for wider code context, teaching models security concepts, and hybrids that join language models with program-analysis tools [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 10].

### Why it matters for your research
This is the key paper for RQ2. It shows that much of the "progress" on old benchmarks comes from wrong labels and leakage. It also gives the only comparison in our set of GPT-4 against fine-tuned models on a de-duplicated, time-split benchmark (RQ1). For your own work, PrimeVul and the pair-wise test are ready-made tools. Never cite a BigVul F1 alone.

### Connections to other papers
- Contradiction C1: fu2023chatgpt finds fine-tuned models far ahead of GPT-4 on BigVul (F1 94% vs 29%) [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4], while here GPT-4 leads on pairs. Ding's own BigVul rows agree with Fu, so the reversal reflects metric and data [I].
- Agreement G2 (noisy labels): risse2025top independently finds only 39–65% of labels correct [@risse2025top, p. 8].
- Agreement G1 (realistic tests collapse scores): see chakraborty2024revisiting, where precision falls to 1–10% [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 7], and lu2025lab.
- Agreement G3 (LLMs over-flag): yildiz2025benchmarking finds "both vulnerable" is 40–95% of LLM failures on pairs [@yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 8].
- Contradiction C7: lu2025lab reports LineVul F1 91.00 on BigVul [@lu2025lab, p. 12], far above Ding's 62.88 for CodeBERT.
- deininger2026open uses PrimeVul without pairs and finds a fine-tuned CodeBERT ahead of all 8 zero-shot LLMs [@deininger2026open, p. 11]. qin2026review repeats this paper's table [@qin2026review, p. 12].

## Top Score on the Wrong Exam: On Benchmarking in Machine Learning for Vulnerability Detection

> **Takeaway:** In three popular C/C++ benchmarks, only 39–65% of functions labelled "vulnerable" really are, and every truly vulnerable function needed code outside it to judge. A simple word-counting model gets close to top published scores, so high benchmark scores are weak evidence that a detector understands vulnerabilities [@risse2025top, p. 8; @risse2025top, p. 9; @risse2025top, p. 11].

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Authors | Niklas Risse, Jing Liu, Marcel Böhme |
| Year | 2025 |
| Venue | Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering (FSE 2025) |
| Status | Peer-reviewed. Our copy is the arXiv version (2408.12986v2), so page numbers follow the arXiv PDF |
| Identifier | DOI 10.1145/3728887; arXiv 2408.12986 |
| Paper type | Literature survey (81 papers), manual expert labelling study, and a simple-model probe experiment |
| Relevance to us | High (RQ2, RQ3, RQ5) |

### In plain words
Machine learning for vulnerability detection (ML4VD) trains models to find security flaws in code. Most of this research asks one question: "given one function, does it contain a flaw?" A function is a small, named block of code. This paper asks whether that question even makes sense. Two security experts checked samples from popular benchmarks by hand. Benchmarks are the shared test collections everyone reports scores on. The authors also built a deliberately simple model that only counts words. If such a model scores well, the benchmark is rewarding shortcuts rather than real understanding.

### How they did it
- Survey: they searched 2020–2024 papers at top software engineering and security venues. Over 2,500 candidates were narrowed to 81 papers; one co-author did the screening [@risse2025top, p. 3; @risse2025top, p. 4].

## Revisiting the Performance of Deep Learning-Based Vulnerability Detection on Realistic Datasets

> **Takeaway:** When four well-known deep-learning detectors scan whole real projects instead of hand-picked functions, their precision falls to 1–10%, so almost every alarm is false. Retraining on realistic data does not fix this, and the small comparison with two fine-tuned LLMs favours neither side clearly [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 7; @chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 9; @chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 12].

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Authors | Partha Chakraborty, Krishna Kanth Arumugam, Mahmoud Alfadel, Meiyappan Nagappan, Shane McIntosh |
| Year | 2024 |
| Venue | IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering |
| Status | Peer-reviewed (journal). Our copy is the arXiv author pre-print (2407.03093v1), so page numbers follow the arXiv PDF |
| Identifier | DOI 10.1109/tse.2024.3423712; arXiv 2407.03093 |
| Paper type | Replication and re-evaluation study with a new dataset (Real-Vul) |
| Relevance to us | High (RQ1, RQ2, RQ4, RQ5) |

### In plain words
Deep-learning (DL) detectors are neural networks trained on many examples of vulnerable and safe code. Some reported scores up to 99%. But they were tested on functions taken from code changes that fixed flaws, with roughly as many vulnerable as safe examples. Real use is different. A tool scans every function in a project, and vulnerable ones are rare. The share of truly vulnerable code is called prevalence. This paper builds a test set, Real-Vul, that mimics a whole-project scan. It then re-tests four detectors on it.

### How they did it
- Detectors: LineVul, which reads code as a sequence of words using the CodeBERT model, and three graph-based models (DeepWukong, ReVeal, IVDetect) [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 4; @chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 5]. Graph-based models turn code into a network of statements and data flows.
- Step 1: re-run each model on its original dataset with a random 80/20 split [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 5; @chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 6].
- Step 2: test those models on Real-Vul (RQ1). Step 3: retrain them on Real-Vul, with and without balancing the classes (RQ2) [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 6; @chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 8].
- Step 4: side analyses, including "dead-code" augmentation, results per weakness group and severity, and two fine-tuned LLMs [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 10; @chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 12]. Dead-code augmentation adds harmless unused code to training examples so the model learns to ignore surface details.
- No static analysis tool was tested [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 13].

### Data and setup
- Real-Vul uses the 10 projects with the most vulnerabilities in the BigVul dataset, including Chromium, Linux, FFmpeg and OpenSSL. They cover 73% of BigVul's vulnerable samples [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 3; @chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 4].
- It has 5,528 vulnerable functions (4,418 train, 1,110 test) and 1,682,713 "uncertain" functions (769,464 train, 913,249 test) [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 4].
- "Uncertain" means every other function in the project snapshot that does not match a known vulnerable function. These are not proven safe [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 4].
- Time split: vulnerable functions are sorted by fix date; the first 80% train the model and the last 20% test it [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 4].
- Training was not repeated; the authors say repeats were not feasible [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 13]. LLM fine-tuning settings are not reported [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 12]. Data and scripts are released [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 2].

### Key findings
- [V] On their original data, DeepWukong reaches F1 93% and LineVul 90% [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 6]. F1 balances precision (share of alarms that are real) and recall (share of real flaws found).
- [V] On Real-Vul, precision falls to 1% (DeepWukong, LineVul), 2% (IVDetect) and 10% (ReVeal), while recall stays at 80–90%. F1 is 2–17% [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 7].
- [V] Precision drops by up to 95 percentage points and F1 by up to 91 points [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 1; @chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 7].
- [V] Retrained on Real-Vul as is, DeepWukong and LineVul label everything as not vulnerable: F1 0% and AUC 50% [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 8]. AUC measures how well a model ranks vulnerable above safe code; 50% is coin-flip level.
- [V] Retrained on balanced data, F1 is 2–36% and AUC 51.3–52.3% [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 9].
- [V] Dead-code augmentation lifts LineVul F1 from 20% to 46% and AUC from 51.4% to 81.8% [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 10].
- [V] Fine-tuned CodeLlama reaches F1 42% and AUC 67%; Mixtral reaches F1 46% and AUC 71%. [A] The authors conclude that LineVul outperforms general LLMs [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 12].
- [V] Information-leak flaws are found best (F1 up to 33.6%). High-severity flaws are hardest (F1 9.06–10.89%) [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 11].

### Limitations and weaknesses
- [A] The authors note that some BigVul labels may be wrong, only 10 projects are used, "uncertain" functions may hide real flaws, balancing used one random sample, and only DL models were tested [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 13].
- [I] Some numbers do not fit together. IVDetect shows precision 39% and recall 63% but F1 24% [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 6]. Project sizes total 270,919 functions, while the text gives 1,682,713 uncertain functions [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 4; @chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 13]. The story holds, but exact figures are less reliable.
- [I] The LLM comparison is thin. Mixtral's F1 (46%) equals augmented LineVul's; only AUC favours LineVul. The LLM results also seem to come from a less imbalanced test set, which is not described [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 10; @chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 12].
- [I] Vulnerable labels come from BigVul, where an independent audit found only 39% correct [@risse2025top, p. 8].
- [I] There are no confidence intervals for the main results. False-positive counts use different units per model, so they cannot be compared directly [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 7].

### Gaps and future work this paper leaves open
- Gap G2 (no same-benchmark comparison of LLMs, static analysis and DL on realistic code): [A] the authors themselves ask for static and dynamic analysis tools to be tested on Real-Vul [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 13]. Real-Vul could serve as that benchmark.
- Gap G1 (results not re-scored at realistic prevalence): this paper shows why prevalence matters. Its precision figures are the kind of number most studies never report [I].
- [A] Other author directions: better detection of high-severity flaws and better LLM specificity, meaning fewer false alarms on safe code [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 11; @chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 12].

### Why it matters for your research
This is the strongest evidence in our set that realistic prevalence destroys precision (RQ2). It also gives results per weakness group and severity (RQ4). If you compare tools, always report precision at a realistic share of vulnerable code, not only F1 on balanced data.

### Connections to other papers
- Agreement G1 (realistic evaluation collapses performance): ding2025vulnerability finds the same with cleaner labels [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]; lu2025lab finds ReVeal and LineVul at F1 3.47–8.65 on 2025 vulnerabilities [@lu2025lab, p. 13].
- Agreement G2 (noisy labels): this paper's 15% inconsistency in ReVeal [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 3] sits beside risse2025top's 39–65% correct labels [@risse2025top, p. 8].
- ding2025vulnerability focuses on wrong labels and copies; this paper focuses on prevalence. Together they explain most of the gap between lab and real scores [I].

Project sizes total 270,919 functions, while the text gives 1,682,713 uncertain functions [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 4; @chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 13]. The story holds, but exact figures are less reliable.
- [I] The LLM comparison is thin. Mixtral's F1 (46%) equals augmented LineVul's; only AUC favours LineVul. The LLM results also seem to come from a less imbalanced test set, which is not described [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 10; @chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 12].
- [I] Vulnerable labels come from BigVul, where an independent audit found only 39% correct [@risse2025top, p. 8].
- [I] There are no confidence intervals for the main results. False-positive counts use different units per model, so they cannot be compared directly [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 7].

### Gaps and future work this paper leaves open
- Gap G2 (no same-benchmark comparison of LLMs, static analysis and DL on realistic code): [A] the authors themselves ask for static and dynamic analysis tools to be tested on Real-Vul [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 13]. Real-Vul could serve as that benchmark.
- Gap G1 (results not re-scored at realistic prevalence): this paper shows why prevalence matters. Its precision figures are the kind of number most studies never report [I].
- [A] Other author directions: better detection of high-severity flaws and better LLM specificity, meaning fewer false alarms on safe code [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 11; @chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 12].

### Why it matters for your research
This is the strongest evidence in our set that realistic prevalence destroys precision (RQ2). It also gives results per weakness group and severity (RQ4). If you compare tools, always report precision at a realistic share of vulnerable code, not only F1 on balanced data.

### Connections to other papers
- Agreement G1 (realistic evaluation collapses performance): ding2025vulnerability finds the same with cleaner labels [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]; lu2025lab finds ReVeal and LineVul at F1 3.47–8.65 on 2025 vulnerabilities [@lu2025lab, p. 13].
- Agreement G2 (noisy labels): this paper's 15% inconsistency in ReVeal [@chakraborty2024revisiting, p. 3] sits beside risse2025top's 39–65% correct labels [@risse2025top, p. 8].
- ding2025vulnerability focuses on wrong labels and copies; this paper focuses on prevalence. Together they explain most of the gap between lab and real scores [I].
